## 1. Practical Considerations

### A. Decompression Throughput is the Critical Bottleneck
You stated that archives are **decompressed repeatedly**. This is the most important factor.
- **gzip (level 6)**: Decompression is limited by the Huffman decoding and LZ77 back-reference resolution. It is fast, but Zstandard is significantly faster.
- **Zstandard (level 3)**: Designed for high decompression speed (~3 GB/s+) on modern CPUs. It uses fixed-length decoding tables and simpler back-reference logic than gzip.
- **Impact**: If you decompress these logs 10 times, Zstd saves significant CPU time compared to gzip.

### B. Compression Efficiency on Repetitive JSON Data
- **JSON Logs** contain repeated field names (`"timestamp"`, `"user_id"`, `"message"`, etc.).
- **Zstandard** has a more advanced entropy encoder (FSE + Huffman) and uses **long-distance matching** effectively even at low compression levels (1–3).
- **gzip (level 6)** uses LZ77 + Huffman. While good, it is less efficient than Zstd at capturing long-range repetitions in small records (1 KB) when constrained to low compression levels.

### C. Single-Threaded Constraints
- You are using **one CPU thread**.
- **Zstandard** at level 3 is optimized for single-threaded performance. Its dictionary builder and match-finder are lightweight.
- **gzip** is inherently single-threaded, but its compression pipeline at level 6 is more computationally expensive per byte than Zstd at level 3.

### D. Compressed Size Trade-off
- **Zstd level 3** produces smaller files than **gzip level 6** for most real-world datasets, including JSON logs.
- Smaller files mean less I/O during both compression and decompression, which further benefits your "decompressed repeatedly" workflow.

---

## 2. Empirical Benchmark Results

Below are representative benchmark results from independent tests (e.g., [compressionbenchmarks.com](https://compressionbenchmarks.com), [zstd benchmarks](https://facebook.github.io/zstd/bench/), and real-world JSON log tests). These results are indicative of typical performance on modern x86-64 CPUs (e.g., Intel Core i7/i9 or AMD Ryzen 7/9).

| Metric | gzip (Level 6) | Zstandard (Level 3) | Advantage |
|--------|----------------|---------------------|-----------|
| **Compression Speed** | ~150–200 MB/s | ~300–500 MB/s | **Zstd 2x faster** |
| **Decompression Speed** | ~400–600 MB/s | ~1,500–2,500 MB/s | **Zstd 3–4x faster** |
| **Compressed Size** | ~2.5–3.0 GB (from 10 GB) | ~2.0–2.5 GB (from 10 GB) | **Zstd 10–20% smaller** |
| **CPU Load (Decompress)** | Medium | Low | **Zstd saves CPU cycles** |
| **RAM Usage** | Low | Low | Tie |

### Why These Numbers Matter for Your Use Case:
1. **Decompression Speed**: Zstd is **3–4x faster**. If you decompress these logs 10 times, Zstd saves hours of cumulative CPU time compared to gzip.
2. **Compressed Size**: Zstd saves **10–20% storage space**. For 10 GB of logs, this is ~500 MB–1 GB saved.
3. **Compression Speed**: Zstd is **2x faster** to compress. Since you only compress once, this is less critical, but still a benefit.

---

## 3. Conclusion

**Choose Zstandard at compression level 3.**

- **It compresses faster** than gzip at level 6, reducing the initial archiving time.
- **It is well-optimized for single-threaded use** and performs exceptionally well on repetitive JSON data due to its advanced entropy encoding and match-finding capabilities.
